The daxophone is a wooden electronic experimental instrument invented by Hans Reichel in Germany and a friction idiophone, Hornbostel–Sachs 132.1. It is built from a wooden tongue about 330 mm long fixed to a wooden base that houses a contact microphone, with a curved wooden strip, the dax, pressed against the tongue to change the pitch. It is mostly played by bowing the free end of the tongue with a double bass bow, though it can also be struck or plucked, and the vibration is picked up and amplified through the base. It first appeared on Hans Reichel's 1987 album, and it has also been used in the scores of the films Smile, The Watchers and The Worm.

演奏時，木塊底座可固定於三腳架或夾在桌面，舌片伸出自由端。通常以低音提琴弓拉奏自: In playing, the wooden base can be fixed to a tripod or clamped to a table top, with the tongue sticking out at its free end. It is usually bowed at the free end with a double bass bow, though it can also be struck or plucked, so that the vibration passes to the base and is amplified by the contact microphone. A beginner can first bow the free end, then use the dax to stop the tongue at different lengths to change the pitch; one side carries frets at random logarithmic spacing, and the other is fretless and covered with cardboard, giving a softer tone and being the side more often used for tonal playing of known works.

Harder tongues of ebony or oak give a rounder tone. The other key part, the dax, is sanded to a curve with cardboard on one side; the source does not state its remaining materials.
達克索風琴可見於實驗音樂、電影配樂與錄音作品。Hans Reichel 1987: The daxophone appears in experimental music, film scores and recordings. Hans Reichel's 1987 album The Dawn of Dachsman was its first use in a musical work; the horror film Smile uses it as the lead instrument, the supernatural thriller The Watchers uses it on almost every track and was the first to build an orchestral texture from daxophone parts, and the short film The Worm scores its soundtrack for daxophone and choir. There are also solo, live and light-opera recordings.

Its timbre is broad and often voice-like and comic, and it changes with the shape of the tongue and the wood; denser woods such as ebony and oak give a softer sound. It sounds by rubbing the wooden tongue with a double bass bow, though it can also be struck or plucked, and the vibration passes to the base and is picked up and amplified by contact microphones; the source does not describe how the volume is controlled. Reichel recorded how to make one in downloadable drawings and supplied the tongue shapes as a font file. In 2022 Smile used it as its main instrumentation, and in 2024 The Watchers was the first to build an orchestral texture from several daxophones, the instruments made by John C. L.
